text:
He figured the day had turned chill, and also felt a bit alone.
Today, I'll light a fire, he thought. He laid dry sticks together and lit them.
not a fire that devours but the one that allows, not a fire that scorches but the one that allows.
Even here, he said, there was a home, and people arrived one by one. Once the cold hands came out from their pockets, that's how stories began—
The sun and the moon tenderly exchanged goodbye, beyond the fence, the weeds were growing, a stray dog retrieved its soul, returning home,
while not-yet-born me— the self that died inside, I lulled and fell asleep.
The fire—extinguished long ago— but certain things did not cease. The fire hadn't hushed, not even a little.
Covered head to toe in flour, I stepped into the square to bring my sorrow into view.
Yesterday, I hid my umbrella in my bag and took the rain on, to proclaim: I do not shatter. I do not disintegrate in the rain. But my bloated, engorged feet spill out from my boots, and no one ever asks if I am okay.
To let my secret out, I left my notebook on the bus, to declare my doorbell was never broken, I hammered nails into the wall even past midnight.
I'm the one effaced. Someone planted the wrong seed, no doubt. My plan to be beautiful has fallen apart. Still, I grow—though warped and out of shape.
With every cough, white powder bursts and flutters. See—this is the color and texture of my soul. You can touch it. Right here.
Only the long silence feels kind. Should I quit it all? I whisper— one drenched dog snaps into a violent spin before my eyes, a blast of droplets erupting, flying in all directions.
That very dog—as if to say it is alive— wades into the muddy pool on its own feet, with joy.
I walked to completely lose myself. Wrote hill and believed it to be one.
Then an unexpected hill would unfold. That day, too, I was walking a hill.
A slope, relatively gentle. Sunlight, enough. A joy in being fully blessed.
After a while, a hollow appeared. I lifted my head to see there were puddles in every direction.
I watched the hill's feeling. A life, so many puddles. A summer where the feet sink, sink. What made you like this?
The hill, close to tears, said the white rabbit hasn't been seen in a while.
After that came the descent. Night came fast, too fast to bear. The hill knew it still had many rabbits inside—but knew, too,
that after stillness always comes storm, that summer exists only to burn everything.
Was it the rabbit we lost? While chasing, as if being chased,
among countless hills, I wondered why it had to be this one.
Even just the fact of going can fold a stretch of time in half. Unfold it, and the landscape is no longer the same.
